draft.title: Medical radioisotopes
card: A radioisotope is an unstable isotope that emits radiation. Doctors use some of them to find cancers and some to treat them.
a radioisotope is given to the patient, and a detector outside the body picks up the radiation it emits. This can show where a tumour is.
a radioisotope is placed in or near a tumour, or given so that it gathers there. Its radiation damages the cancer cells.
Radiation also harms healthy tissue. Doctors weigh the damage to diseased cells against the harm to healthy tissue when they choose an isotope and dose.
draft.remember: Radioisotopes help to find and treat cancers, but healthy tissue can be harmed, so the risk is weighed.

a.q: Why do doctors weigh the benefits and risks when using a radioisotope to treat a tumour?
opts: Its radiation can also harm healthy tissue
It cannot damage the cancer cells at all
It only works when used to find tumours
Healthy tissue is never exposed to radiation
a.why: Radiation damages diseased cells, which is the aim, but it can also harm healthy tissue nearby. The card does not say it fails to damage cancer cells, as treatment depends on that damage.
a.clue: Radiation does not choose which cells it hits.

b.q: Sam has a radioisotope injected, and a detector outside his body records where it gathers. What is this use of the radioisotope for?
opts: Finding a tumour
Treating a tumour
Removing healthy tissue
Making his body stable
b.why: A detector outside the body picks up the emitted radiation, which shows where the isotope has gathered. That is for finding a tumour. Treating relies on radiation damaging the cancer cells.
b.clue: A detector only records, it does not damage cells.

a.best: Its radiation can also harm healthy tissue

problems.detail: The three wrong options all use absolute words ('never', 'cannot ... at all', 'only'), while the right option is the only one with the hedge 'can'. A student could pick it by spotting that pattern without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card is accurate and both intended answers are correct. One minor issue: in question a the right option is the only one without an absolute word, so it stands out from the distractors.

card: A radioisotope is an unstable isotope that emits radiation. Doctors use some of them to find cancers and some to treat them.

proposal.remember: Radioisotopes help to find and treat cancers, but healthy tissue can be harmed, so the risk is weighed.

a.q: Why do doctors weigh the benefits and risks when using a radioisotope to treat a tumour?
opts: Its radiation damages healthy tissue as well as cancer cells
Its radiation damages cancer cells but spares healthy tissue
Its radiation is too weak to damage the cancer cells
Its radiation damages healthy tissue but not cancer cells
a.why: Treatment works because the radiation damages cancer cells, but it also harms healthy tissue, so doctors weigh one against the other. The option saying it spares healthy tissue is wrong: if it did, there would be no harm to weigh.
a.clue: Radiation does not choose which cells it hits.

b.q: Sam has a radioisotope injected, and a detector outside his body records where it gathers. What is this use of the radioisotope for?
opts: Finding a tumour
Treating a tumour
Removing healthy tissue
Making his body stable
b.why: A detector outside the body picks up the emitted radiation, which shows where the isotope has gathered. That is for finding a tumour. Treating relies on radiation damaging the cancer cells, not on recording where it goes.
b.clue: A detector records radiation, it does not damage cells.

a.best: Its radiation damages healthy tissue as well as cancer cells
